dek: The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28, but two officials wanted a hike and markets are eyeing Dec. 9.

slides.label: The hold
slides.text: Last Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate at *3.75% to 4%*. That follows September, when the Fed raised rates for the *first time since 2023*.

slides.label: The split
slides.text: The vote was *10 to 2*. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both wanted another quarter-point hike right away. Two dissenters pushing higher is a *loud signal*.

slides.label: December
slides.text: The next meeting is *Dec. 9*. Yahoo Finance reported bond traders pricing in about an *85% chance* of a quarter-point hike. Chair Kevin Warsh would not pre-commit.

slides.label: Credit cards
slides.text: Card APRs already rose after the September hike, and most issuers won't change rates on a hold alone. The pause is *breathing room, not relief*. Another hike likely makes card debt *pricier again*.

slides.label: Savings
slides.text: The upside: savings yields held roughly steady, per Money Under 30. High-yield savings and CDs opened after September should keep paying *similar rates for now*. Cash earning *close to zero* works for the bank.

slides.label: Mortgages
slides.text: The 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above *5%*. Freddie Mac's 30-year average came in at *7.24%*, a second straight weekly dip. Purchase applications run *18% below* last year's pace.

slides.label: New York
slides.text: City Hall's True Cost of Living Measure found *62%* of New Yorkers can't cover basic expenses even working full time. A typical family needs about *$40,000 more* a year to make ends meet.

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: Higher for longer is now the environment. The weeks before Dec. 9 are for basics, like knowing card rates and running honest numbers. Wealth comes from *a hundred boring moves*. *Not financial advice*.

The Fed held rates last week. That sounds like nothing happened. It was a hold with a lean, and the lean is toward higher.

On Oct. 28 the Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%, after raising in September for the first time since 2023. The vote was 10 to 2, and both dissenters, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, wanted a hike right away. Bond traders are pricing in about an 85% chance of a quarter-point hike on Dec. 9. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above 5%, and Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage average sits at 7.24%. Card APRs already rose after September, while savings yields held roughly steady.

Here at home, City Hall found 62% of New Yorkers can't cover basic expenses even working full time.

The other side: Chair Kevin Warsh would not pre-commit to December, and mortgage rates dipped for a second straight week. General information, not financial advice.
